newsitem.title: USA: U.S. silent on whether it backs Nigerian action.
newsitem.headline: U.S. silent on whether it backs Nigerian action.

text.p: The United States on Monday was silent on whether it supported Nigeria's battle to overturn a coup against Sierra Leone's democratic government as more evacuations of Americans and foreigners were being considered.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry, asked whether the United States supported Nigeria's efforts, would not answer either way, saying Washington was encouraging regional efforts to arrange a ceasefire.

"There's continuing violence there, and we are interested in diminishing the violence and seeing if this fragile ceasefire that they've been working on can't be fully implemented. We are concerned for the safety of those remaining in the capital city. We are monitoring very carefully the situation on the ground," McCurry told reporters.

Another White House official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said U.S. spokesmen were purposely circumspect in discussing the action by Nigerian troops in reaction to the military coup eight days ago that threw out democratically elected President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah.

"What we care about are several things -- the restoration of democracy and safety of our citizens and the well-being of the people of Sierra Leone. We're not injecting ourselves as a player. We're being quite clear that we think it's very important that democracy be restored and that violence be stopped," this official said.
Meantime, U.S. officials were looking at the possibility of a further evacuation of Americans and other foreigners from the Sierra Leone capital Freetown.

U.S. helicopters evacuated some 400 Americans and 900 other foreigners on Friday and on Sunday to a warship stationed offshore shortly before fighting erupted between Nigerian intervention forces and Sierra Leone soldiers.

State Department spokesman John Dinger said between 12 and 30 Americans and around 200 other foreign nationals were reported to be still holed up in Freetown's Mammy Yoko hotel, which has been a centre of the clashes.

U.S. diplomats aboard the U.S. warship, the helicopter carrier Kearsarge, and the commander of U.S. forces there "will make a judgment call on whether and when further evacuations can take place," Dinger told a new briefing.
He said the Kearsarge "will remain in the area, pending a determination of whether another evacuation from Freetown is possible."
Nigeria is joined by other West African forces in trying to overturn the coup, whose leaders have been backed by rebel forces in Sierra Leone.
The United States closed its embassy in Freetown on last Friday and evacuated all diplomats. Ambassador John Hirsch and deputy chief of mission Ann Wright are aboard the Kearsarge.

President Bill Clinton, in a letter to House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich and Sen. Strom Thurmond, the Senate's oldest member, said there was no evidence U.S. citizens were being targeted but that violence in Freetown subjected them to continued risks.
Clinton said U.S. forces would leave Sierre Leone "as soon as evacuation operations are complete and enhanced security and locations in and around Freetown is no longer required."
